input.question: How Small Would Something Have to be in Order to Orbit Around Someone in Space?
input.ground_truth: There is no mass limit, but both the person and other object orbit the center of mass of the system. For a very light object, the center of mass will be inside the person. For heavier and heavier objects, the center of mass will gradually move farther toward the other object, until for equal mass the point is exactly in the middle. [Watch these animations](_URL_1_) to see what I mean. Based on the masses and distances of the objects, speed is the critical quantity. To orbit a 100 kg person 1 meter away circularly, a small object should move at about [80 microns/s](_URL_0_), or 1 orbit every 21.4 hours.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How Small Would Something Have to be in Order to Orbit Around Someone in Space?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a tiny marble and you throw it around your friend while you’re both floating in space. If you throw the marble just right—not too slow and not too fast—it will go around your friend instead of flying away or hitting them.

But in space, there’s no air to slow things down, so even a very small thing, like a grain of sand, can go around a bigger thing if it’s moving at the right speed and not too close. However, if it’s too close, the bigger thing’s gravity will pull it in and it won’t orbit—it’ll just fall.

So, something can be as small as a pebble or even smaller and still orbit, as long as it moves in the right way and isn’t too close. But if it’s too tiny, like a single atom, it’s so light that it might just float away or get pulled in right away.

So, it doesn’t have to be big to orbit—it just has to be moving the right way!
